6. Although the authors state that “the system demonstrated its tactile-visual signal
recognition applications for environment adaption and interaction in metaverse
scenarios.” the manuscript does not describe how metaverse scenarios are realized.
Simple dynamic trajectory recognition alone is insufficient to justify such claims.
Response: We greatly appreciate your valuable comments. The metaverse is a digital
three-dimensional space that integrates virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR),
artificial intelligence (AI), and Internet of Things (IoT) technologies. It expands human
perception capabilities through multi-sensory real-time perception and processing
technologies as well as high-precision spatial positioning technologies, thereby
achieving an immersive experience of the deep integration of virtual and real worlds.
Metaverse technology needs to have functions such as multi-modal perception,
wearable integrated perception-processing system, trajectory recognition, and precise
spatial positioning (Supplementary Fig. S32). Our work designed and constructed a
flexible perception-processing-visualization integrated system (FSPVS) based on the
multifunctional properties of MXene and its derivatives, which has the potential to
partially realize certain functionalities (by taking the badminton sports scene as a
conceptual example) that are highly desired in the metaverse.
As a response and to avoid misleading readers, we have modified the corresponding
description of “the system demonstrated its tactile-visual signal recognition
applications for environment adaption and interaction in metaverse scenarios” as
follows: “The system demonstrates its tactile-visual signal recognition capabilities for
environmental adaptation and functionalities that are highly desired in the metaverse.”
and added Supplementary Fig. S32 and corresponding description: “This wearable
system can achieve several key functions including multi-modal perception, integrated
perception-processing architecture, trajectory recognition, and accurate spatial
positioning (Supplementary Fig. S32), which is highly desired for metaverse
applications.” in the manuscript.
Supplementary Fig. S32. Schematic showing the illustration of our simple badminton
example satisfying key requirements that are highly desired in the metaverse in the
future. The metaverse is a digital three-dimensional space that integrates virtual reality
(VR), augmented reality (AR), artificial intelligence (AI), and Internet of Things (IoT)
technologies. It expands human perception capabilities through multi-sensory real-time
perception and processing technologies as well as high-precision spatial positioning
technologies, thereby achieving an immersive experience of the deep integration of
virtual and real worlds. Metaverse technology needs to have functions such as multi-
modal perception, wearability, and integrated perception-processing system, trajectory
recognition, and precise spatial positioning (Supplementary Fig. S32). However,
current technologies are limited by the dispersion and low efficiency of modular design
and information processing architecture, resulting in complex system structures, high
energy consumption, and significant impacts on immersive experience and
interconnection performance. Our work designed and constructed a FSPVS based on
the multifunctional properties of MXene and its derivatives, which has the potential to
partially realize certain functionalities associated with the metaverse. Taking a simple
badminton sports scene as a conceptual example, we proposed a motion scheme of dual-
modal perception-processing-light feedback of touch and vision, fully leveraging the
unique advantages of this system. This system can dynamically recognize the strike
type and racket swing trajectory, and achieve high-precision spatial positioning at the
same time, providing an important reference for building a deeply integrated metaverse
that connects humans, physical environments, and virtual spaces.
7. Simulation experiments lack essential details. Specifically, the datasets and neural
network architecture used for classification and racket trajectory prediction tasks are
not provided.
Response: We greatly appreciate your valuable comments. In the Methods section, we
have supplemented detailed simulation content, including the neural network
architecture and parameter settings. Additionally, in the Supplementary information,
we have offered the dataset construction process for classification tasks and racket
trajectory prediction (Supplementary Figs. S33−S35).
As a response, we have added Supplementary Figs. S33−S35, and added neural
network architecture details to the Methods section:
“Network training
For multimodal Fashion-MNIST recognition: the original 28×28 pixel images were
binarized and restructured into a 196×4 pixel format. Subsequently, the processed
images were read by using a mixed-input “EEOO” mode. The covered yellow pixels
on the left half could only be sensed via electrical pulses from tactile signals, whereas
the purple pixels represent their absence; all pixels on the right half indicate the absence
of an electrical pulse. The yellow pixels on the right half correspond to light pulse inputs.
A total of 196 input channels were fed into corresponding memory units for processing.
Then, a single-layer fully connected neural network is employed to perform the
multimodal Fashion-MNIST recognition task.
For strike types recognition: the experimental participant swung the racket with varying
types, and raw data was collected. The one-dimensional strike-type data (2000) was
converted into a four-row pixel format (4×500) through cropping and binarization.
Subsequently, the strike type data are fed into the AOS reservoir in electrical mode for
computation. The AOS reservoir in the electrical mode consists of 500 storage devices
that serve as reservoir nodes. Then, a single-layer fully connected neural network with
500 input nodes was designed to perform the strike types recognition task. For racket
swing trajectory recognition: image sequences of each racket trajectory were captured,
and the frame difference method combined with binarization processing was applied to
generate image sequences. Each input image (56×56) was divided into four consecutive
pixel rows (4×3136), spanning from the leftmost to the rightmost column in a top-down
manner. Subsequently, the swing trajectory information was fed into the AOS reservoir
in optical mode for computation. The AOS reservoir in the optical mode consists of
3136 storage devices that serve as reservoir nodes. Their conductance values are
programmed and calibrated based on experimentally measured data from individual
devices. Then, a single-layer fully connected neural network with 3136 input nodes was
designed to perform the racket swing trajectory recognition task. The readout layer was
implemented in software, and the model was trained using the Adam optimizer’s
gradient descent algorithm (with an initial learning rate of 0.001) to minimize
classification cross-entropy loss. Finally, the data were divided into training and test
sets to evaluate the performance of the model.” in the manuscript.
